chapter_note.about: Logistic regression predicts the probability of class 1. It computes a score from the inputs, passes it through the S-shaped sigmoid, and predicts class 1 when the probability is at least a half, which is the same as the score being at least zero. That makes the decision boundary a straight line. The weights are found by minimising the log-loss, which is the same as maximum likelihood. GATE tests it through linear separability from plots (does a straight line work?), through reading the model (probabilities, odds, the boundary), and once through precision and recall from a confusion matrix.

chapter_note.simple: Logistic regression answers yes-or-no questions by giving a probability. It adds up the evidence from the inputs into one score, then squeezes that score into a number between 0 and 1 with an S-shaped curve. If the number is at least 0.5 it says yes. Because the score is a plain weighted sum, the line between yes and no is always straight, so it cannot handle patterns like a chessboard. To train it, you punish the model hard for being confidently wrong and nudge the weights downhill. In exams you read the model (probabilities, odds, the boundary), check whether a straight line can split a picture, and sometimes work out precision and recall.

cards.title: Sigmoid
cards.simple: A model's raw score can be any number, like −7 or 12. But a probability must sit between 0 and 1. The sigmoid is a squeezing machine that fixes this. Feed in a huge positive number and it gives out something just under 1. Feed in a huge negative number and it gives something just above 0. Feed in exactly 0 and it gives one half, a coin flip. It works like a dimmer switch: the more you turn it, the brighter the light gets, but it never goes past fully off or fully on. In exam words: $\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$ lies strictly between 0 and 1, and $\sigma(0)=0.5$.
cards.idea: Logistic regression first computes a score $z$ that can be any real number. The **sigmoid** turns that score into a probability. Large positive scores give probabilities near 1, large negative scores give probabilities near 0, and a score of 0 gives exactly 0.5. The curve is S-shaped and always increasing.
cards.definition:
$$\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$$

Symbols: $z$ is the score (any real number), $e\approx2.718$, and $e^{-z}$ means 1 divided by $e^{z}$.

Facts to remember:

- $0<\sigma(z)<1$, and it never equals 0 or 1.
- $\sigma(0)=0.5$.
- Symmetry: $\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)$.
- Slope: $\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\,(1-\sigma(z))$, largest (0.25) at $z=0$.
cards.intuition_full: A probability must live between 0 and 1, but a linear score does not, so we need a smooth, increasing function that maps the whole number line into the open interval (0, 1). The sigmoid is the natural choice because it is the inverse of the log-odds (see the odds card): if the log-odds of class 1 is $z$, then the probability is $\sigma(z)$. Read the formula to see why it behaves. When $z$ is large and positive, $e^{-z}$ is tiny, so the bottom is about 1 and $\sigma\approx1$. When $z$ is large and negative, $e^{-z}$ is huge, so $\sigma\approx0$. At $z=0$ we get $e^0=1$ and $\sigma=1/2$. The symmetry says that flipping the sign of the score swaps the two class probabilities. Far from 0 the curve is almost flat: the slope $\sigma(1-\sigma)$ is tiny, so changing the score barely changes the probability. This is called saturation.

examples.answer: $\sigma=0.5,\ 0.731,\ 0.881,\ 0.269,\ 0.119$. All lie between 0 and 1, and $\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)$.

examples.setup: A model outputs $\sigma(z_1)=0.9$ for some sample. Find $\sigma(-z_1)$, the score $z_1$, and the slope of the sigmoid at $z_1$.
steps: Slope: $\sigma(1-\sigma)=0.9\cdot0.1=0.09$, well below the maximum $0.25$ at $z=0$.

examples.setup: A very confident model has scores $z=10$ and $z=-10$. Find the probabilities and the slope at $z=10$. Does the sigmoid reach 1?
steps: So the curve is almost flat out there, and it never actually reaches 1 or 0.
examples.answer: $\sigma(10)=0.99995$, which is not 1. The slope is almost 0 (saturation), so a confident model barely changes its output when the score moves.

cards.title: Model and decision boundary
cards.simple: Logistic regression gives each point a "how likely is class 1" number, then draws a straight line where that likelihood is exactly 50 percent. Points on one side of the line are predicted as class 1 and points on the other side as class 0. Picture a fence in a field that separates two kinds of animals. The weights decide how the fence is tilted, and the bias slides the fence sideways. The fence is always straight, never curved. In exam words: $P(y=1\mid x)=\sigma(w^\top x+b)$, and the decision boundary is $w^\top x+b=0$.
cards.idea: The model computes a score $z=w^\top x+b$ and outputs $p=\sigma(z)$, the probability of class 1. It predicts class 1 when $p\ge0.5$, which happens exactly when $z\ge0$. The boundary where $p=0.5$ is $w^\top x+b=0$. That is a straight line in 2-D, and a flat plane in higher dimensions.
cards.definition:
$$P(y=1\mid x)=\sigma(w^\top x+b),\qquad \text{boundary: } w^\top x+b=0$$

Symbols: $w$ holds the weights (one per feature), $b$ is the bias (intercept), and $x$ is the input. The vector $w$ points perpendicular to the boundary, so it sets the tilt, and $b$ slides the line sideways.

If you predict class 1 at a threshold $p^*$ other than 0.5, the boundary moves to $z=\ln\frac{p^*}{1-p^*}$ but stays straight.
cards.intuition_full: The rule "$p\ge0.5$" looks curved because of the sigmoid, but the sigmoid is increasing, so $p\ge0.5$ means the same as $z\ge0$. And $z$ is a plain linear function of $x$. The set where a linear function equals 0 is a line (in 2-D) or a plane (in 3-D): flat. That is why logistic regression is called a linear classifier, even though its output curve is S-shaped in $z$. The score $z$ is proportional to the signed distance from the boundary, so points far from it get probabilities near 0 or 1, and points on it get 0.5. If you scale $w$ and $b$ together by 5, the boundary does not move, but the model becomes much more confident.

example.setup: A model has $w=(1,2)$ and $b=-4$. Find the boundary, then classify $A=(1,1)$, $B=(3,2)$ and $C=(2,1)$ and compute their probabilities.
steps: The score is $z=x_1+2x_2-4$. The boundary is $z=0$, the line $x_1+2x_2=4$ (through $(4,0)$ and $(0,2)$).
$A=(1,1)$: $z=1+2-4=-1$, so $p=\sigma(-1)=0.27$. This is below 0.5, so class 0.
$C=(2,1)$: $z=2+2-4=0$, so $p=0.5$. It sits exactly on the boundary.
Change $b$ to $-2$: the boundary becomes $x_1+2x_2=2$. It has the same tilt, slid parallel, and is still a straight line.
example.answer: Boundary $x_1+2x_2=4$. A is class 0 ($p=0.27$), B is class 1 ($p=0.95$), and C is on the line ($p=0.5$).

cards.title: Odds and log-odds
cards.simple: Odds are how bookmakers talk. If the chance of rain is 60 percent, the odds are 3 to 2 in favour: 0.6 of the time yes against 0.4 of the time no. Log-odds is just the natural log of that odds number. Logistic regression has a neat secret: it assumes the log-odds moves in a perfectly straight line with the inputs. Each time an input goes up by one, the log-odds goes up by the weight, which means the odds get multiplied by a fixed factor. In exam words: $\ln\frac{p}{1-p}=w^\top x+b$, and one unit of $x_j$ multiplies the odds by $e^{w_j}$.
cards.idea: Odds compare the chance of yes with the chance of no: $p/(1-p)$. The **log-odds** (or logit) is the log of that. Logistic regression says the log-odds is a plain linear function of the inputs. So adding 1 to a feature adds its weight $w$ to the log-odds, and multiplies the odds by $e^{w}$. This is the easy way to read a logistic regression.
cards.definition:
$$\text{odds}=\frac{p}{1-p},\qquad \text{logit}(p)=\ln\frac{p}{1-p}=w^\top x+b,\qquad p=\frac{\text{odds}}{1+\text{odds}}=\sigma(\text{logit})$$

Symbols: $\ln$ is the natural log. For a feature $x_j$, raising it by 1 (others fixed) adds $w_j$ to the log-odds, so the odds are multiplied by $e^{w_j}$. The logit is the inverse of the sigmoid.
cards.intuition_full: Probabilities are awkward to model with a straight line, because they are stuck between 0 and 1 and a line would eventually cross those walls. Odds run from 0 to infinity, and log-odds run over the whole number line. A straight line can live on the whole number line, so logistic regression lets the line live in log-odds and converts back with the sigmoid. Why logs? Effects of different features multiply on the odds scale, and logs turn multiplication into addition, which a linear model handles. One more picture: equal steps in $x$ give equal steps in log-odds, but not equal steps in probability. The probability changes fastest around 0.5 and slowly near 0 and 1.

example.setup: A probability is $p=0.6$. Find the odds and the log-odds. Then use the model log-odds $z=-1+0.5x$ to find $p$ at $x=2$ and at $x=3$.
steps: Log-odds $=\ln1.5=0.405$. The model says $z=-1+0.5x$ is a straight line in $x$.
At $x=3$: $z=0.5$. The odds are $e^{0.5}=1.649$, so $p=1.649/2.649=0.622$. One more unit of $x$ added $0.5$ to the log-odds and multiplied the odds by $e^{0.5}=1.65$.
example.answer: Odds 1.5 and log-odds 0.405 for $p=0.6$. The model gives $p=0.5$ at $x=2$ and $p=0.622$ at $x=3$.

examples.answer: No. Equal steps in $x$ give equal steps in log-odds, but the probability changes less near 0 and 1.

cards.why: Odds and log-odds are the easiest way to read and to compute with logistic regression, and they connect it to Bayes' theorem. In GATE: the log-odds of a given probability, a probability from log-odds, or the factor by which the odds change per unit of a feature.
how: Probability to odds: $p/(1-p)$.
Odds to log-odds: take $\ln$.
The model's score $z=w^\top x+b$ is the log-odds.
One unit up in $x_j$ multiplies the odds by $e^{w_j}$.
cards.mistake: Saying one unit of $x$ multiplies the probability by $e^{w}$, or adds $w$ to the probability. It is the odds that are multiplied (and the log-odds that get $w$ added). The change in probability depends on where you start.
edge_cases: $p=0.5$ gives odds 1 and log-odds 0.
$p>0.5$ gives odds above 1 and a positive log-odds.
A negative $w$ makes the odds shrink as $x$ grows, as in the exam example.
Odds have no upper limit: odds of 99 means $p=0.99$.
connections: Foundations: Exponents and logarithms covers $e^{w}$ and $\ln$.
Bayes theorem: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio, the same odds idea.
Sigmoid (an earlier card) is the inverse of the logit.

cards.title: Log-loss
cards.simple: Imagine a teacher who marks each guess by how sure you were. If you were 95 percent sure and right, you lose almost nothing. If you were only 60 percent sure and right, you lose a bit more. But if you were 95 percent sure and wrong, you lose a lot. Log-loss is exactly this penalty. It looks at the probability the model gave to the true answer, and it punishes confident mistakes very hard. In exam words: loss $=-\ln$ (the probability given to the true class).
cards.idea: Log-loss scores a probability prediction. Look at the probability the model gave to the **true** class and take $-\ln$ of it. If that probability is near 1, the loss is near 0. If it is small, the loss is large and grows without limit as the probability goes to 0. So a model is punished most for being confidently wrong.
cards.definition:
For one sample with label $y\in\{0,1\}$ and predicted $p=P(y=1)$:
$$L=-\big[\,y\ln p+(1-y)\ln(1-p)\,\big]$$

So $L=-\ln p$ when $y=1$, and $L=-\ln(1-p)$ when $y=0$. Symbols: $\ln$ is the natural log. For many samples, add the losses (or average them, as the question says). Training logistic regression means choosing $w$ and $b$ to minimise the total log-loss.
cards.intuition_full: The formula uses $y$ as a switch. With $y=1$ only the first term survives, and with $y=0$ only the second. In both cases you take $-\ln$ of the probability that the model assigned to what actually happened. Why a log? The probability of a whole dataset is a product of the individual probabilities, and logs turn products into sums. So the total log-loss is minus the log of the dataset's likelihood, and minimising it makes the data as likely as possible (see the maximum likelihood card). The shape matters too. As $p\to0$ for the true class, $-\ln p\to\infty$: a model that says "impossible" about something that happens is punished without limit. That keeps probabilities honest. Squared error would punish a confident mistake by at most 1.

example.setup: Four predictions. (a) $y=1$, $p=0.6$. (b) $y=0$, $p=0.6$. (c) $y=1$, $p=0.95$. (d) $y=1$, $p=0.05$. Find each loss, and the total and mean.
steps: (b) $y=0$: loss $=-\ln(1-0.6)=-\ln0.4=0.916$. The same $p$ costs more when it sits on the wrong side.

example.answer: Losses $0.511,\ 0.916,\ 0.051,\ 2.996$. Total $4.474$, mean $1.12$. The one confident mistake supplies most of it.

cards.title: Gradient
cards.simple: To train the model, you nudge each weight in the direction that lowers the log-loss. For logistic regression the nudge has a lovely simple shape. Take how wrong the probability was (prediction minus truth), multiply it by the input, and move the weight the opposite way. If the model said 0.9 but the truth was 0, the error is 0.9 and the weight is pushed down. If it said 0.1 but the truth was 1, the error is −0.9 and the weight is pushed up. In exam words: $\partial L/\partial w=(p-y)\,x$ and $w\leftarrow w-\eta\,(p-y)\,x$.
cards.idea: Gradient descent trains logistic regression. Once the derivative is worked out, the gradient of the log-loss with respect to a weight is simply **(prediction − label) × input**, that is $(p-y)\,x$. The bias has the same gradient with $x$ replaced by 1. You update each weight by subtracting $\eta$ times its gradient. It has the same shape as the rule for linear regression, with the sigmoid output $p$ in place of the line's output.
cards.definition:
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_j}=(p-y)\,x_j,\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=p-y,\qquad w_j\leftarrow w_j-\eta\,(p-y)\,x_j$$

Symbols: $p=\sigma(w^\top x+b)$, $y$ is the label (0 or 1), and $\eta$ is the learning rate. For a batch, add (or average) $(p-y)x$ over the samples.

Sign trap: the gradient is $(p-y)x$, not $(y-p)x$. The update then subtracts it.
cards.intuition_full: The derivative of $-\ln\sigma(z)$ looks messy, but it simplifies. The sigmoid's slope $\sigma(1-\sigma)$ cancels against the slope of the log, and what is left is $p-y$ as the slope with respect to the score $z$. The chain rule then gives an extra factor $x$ for the weight, and a factor 1 for the bias. Read it as "error times input". The error $p-y$ is positive when the model is too keen on class 1 and negative when it is too shy. A big input means that weight had a lot of say in the mistake, so it gets a big correction. Squared error would multiply in an extra factor $p(1-p)$, which vanishes when the model is confidently wrong, so learning would stall. Log-loss keeps a full-strength gradient exactly when it is needed.

example.setup: One sample $x=3$ with label $y=0$. Weights $w=0.5$ and $b=-1$, learning rate $\eta=0.1$. Do one gradient step on the log-loss.
steps: Gradients: $\partial L/\partial w=(p-y)x=0.622\cdot3=1.867$ and $\partial L/\partial b=0.622$.
New score $z=0.313\cdot3-1.062=-0.122$, so $p=0.469$. The loss falls from $0.974$ to $0.634$.
example.answer: $w=0.313$ and $b=-1.062$. The probability of class 1 dropped from 0.622 to 0.469, closer to the true label 0.

cards.title: Linear separability
cards.simple: Logistic regression can draw only one straight line. If the two kinds of points can be split by a single straight line, it can do the job. If they are mixed so that no straight line can put one kind on each side, it fails. The classic example is a chessboard pattern: two circles on one diagonal and two squares on the other. Any straight line leaves a circle and a square on the same side. The fix is to give the model a new feature, like the product of the two coordinates, so that in the new picture a straight line works. In exam words: logistic regression has a linear boundary, so XOR and "surrounded" classes cannot be fitted with the raw features.
cards.idea: A dataset is **linearly separable** if one straight line (or flat plane) puts all of one class on one side and all of the other class on the other. Logistic regression with raw features has a linear boundary, so it can fit only separable data perfectly. XOR patterns and a class surrounded by another are not separable. Adding a derived feature, such as a product or a square, can make them separable.
cards.definition:
Separable means there exist $w$ and $b$ with $w^\top x+b>0$ for every class-1 point and $<0$ for every class-0 point.

Quick test: the two classes are separable exactly when their **convex hulls** do not overlap. The convex hull is the shape you get by stretching a rubber band around the points of one class.

Adding a feature $\phi(x)$, such as $x_1x_2$ or $x_1^2$, gives a linear boundary in the new features, which is a curved boundary in the old ones.
cards.intuition_full: Two classes can be separated by a line exactly when you can slip a straight stick between them. In the XOR picture, the segment joining the two class-0 points and the segment joining the two class-1 points cross in the middle. A line that keeps both class-0 points on one side keeps their whole segment there, including the crossing point, so the class-1 segment cannot lie wholly on the other side. For a class surrounded by another, the inner point lies inside the rubber band of the outer points, so it can never be split from them. A new feature changes the picture. With the product $x_1x_2$ (after centring), the XOR points move to different heights, and a flat plane at the right height splits them. The boundary in the original plane is then curved, even though the model is still linear in its inputs.

example.setup: Class 0: A $=(1,1)$ and B $=(3,3)$. Class 1: C $=(1,3)$ and D $=(3,1)$. Can logistic regression on $(x_1,x_2)$ separate them? Which added feature fixes it?
steps: Plot the four points. Class 0 sits on one diagonal and class 1 on the other.
Try $x_1=2$ (vertical) and $x_2=2$ (horizontal). Each leaves one point of each class on both sides. Both fail.
Try $x_1+x_2=2.5$. It isolates A, but B, C and D are on the other side and still mixed. It fails too.
Reason: segment AB and segment CD cross at $(2,2)$. No line can keep A and B on one side and C and D on the other.
Add the feature $x_1x_2$. The score $z=2x_1+2x_2-x_1x_2-4$ gives A: $2+2-1-4=-1$, B: $6+6-9-4=-1$, C: $2+6-3-4=+1$, D: $6+2-3-4=+1$. A linear model in the three features separates them.
example.answer: Not separable with $(x_1,x_2)$ alone (XOR). Adding $x_1x_2$ makes it separable.

examples.setup: Which datasets can logistic regression on the raw features $(x_1,x_2)$ classify with 100% training accuracy? (i) Circles at $(0,4),(1,5),(2,4)$ and squares at $(3,0),(4,1),(5,0)$. steps: Rule: the data are separable exactly when the convex hulls of the two classes do not overlap.
(i) The circles all have $x_2\ge4$ and the squares all have $x_2\le1$. The line $x_2=2.5$ separates them. Yes.
(ii) The squares form a diamond around $(3,3)$. Their average is $\big(\tfrac{3+1+5+3}4,\ \tfrac{5+3+3+1}4\big)=(3,3)$, which is the circle. The circle lies inside their hull. No.

examples.setup: Take dataset (ii) from the exam example: a circle at $(3,3)$ surrounded by four squares. Add the feature $r^2=(x_1-3)^2+(x_2-3)^2$. Is it now separable?

examples.answer: Yes. The model is linear in $r^2$, and the boundary in the original plane is a circle.

cards.title: Maximum likelihood
cards.simple: Training means choosing the settings that make the data you actually saw as likely as possible. If a coin landed heads 3 times out of 5, the best guess for its chance of heads is 3 out of 5, because that setting makes "what we saw" the most probable. That idea is called maximum likelihood. For logistic regression it is the same as making the total log-loss as small as possible. There is a catch: if one straight line can split the data perfectly, the weights keep growing forever, because bigger weights always make the data look more certain. In exam words: fit by maximum likelihood, which means minimise log-loss (convex, no closed form), and on separable data the weights diverge.
cards.idea: The **likelihood** of the data is the product of the probabilities the model gave to each observed label. Maximum likelihood picks the weights that make this product as large as possible. Taking logs and flipping the sign, that is the same as minimising the total log-loss. The loss is convex, so gradient descent reaches the single best answer, but there is no closed formula. If the data are perfectly separable, bigger weights always help, so no best finite weights exist.
cards.definition:
$$L(w,b)=\prod_i p_i^{\,y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i},\qquad -\ln L=\sum_i\big[-y_i\ln p_i-(1-y_i)\ln(1-p_i)\big]$$

Symbols: $p_i=\sigma(w^\top x_i+b)$, and $\prod$ means "multiply over all samples". Maximising $L$ is the same as minimising $-\ln L$, the total log-loss.

Facts: the log-loss is convex in $(w,b)$, so there is one global minimum. There is no closed form. For an intercept-only model the answer is $p=\bar y$ (the fraction of ones), so $b=\ln\frac{\bar y}{1-\bar y}$. With separable data the weights diverge to infinity, and an L2 penalty keeps them finite.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the model as a story generator. Each choice of weights is a different story about how likely each label was. The likelihood scores each story by how probable it makes the real data, and we pick the story that makes the real data least surprising. With independent samples, the probabilities multiply, and logs turn the product into a sum, which is the total log-loss. Why no closed form? In linear regression the loss is a quadratic bowl whose bottom can be written down. Here the sigmoid inside the log makes the equations impossible to solve in one line, so we iterate (gradient descent or Newton's method). Why divergence on separable data? If a line separates the data, doubling $w$ pushes every probability further toward its correct end, so the loss falls again. It only reaches 0 at infinite weights, so there is no best finite answer until you add a penalty.

example.setup: Five labels: $1,0,0,1,1$. The model gives every sample the same probability $p$ (intercept only). Which $p$ maximises the likelihood?
steps: Every sample has the same $p=P(y=1)$. The labels are 1, 0, 0, 1, 1.
The smallest is at $p=0.6$, which is 3 ones out of 5. Maximum likelihood equals minimum log-loss.

examples.setup: Two training points: $x=-1$ with $y=0$, and $x=1$ with $y=1$. Fit $p=\sigma(wx)$ with no bias by maximum likelihood. What happens to the loss as $w$ grows?
steps: By symmetry both samples have the same loss $\ln(1+e^{-w})$, so the total is $2\ln(1+e^{-w})$.
The loss keeps falling and reaches 0 only at $w=\infty$. There is no best finite $w$.
examples.answer: The loss decreases forever, so the maximum-likelihood weight does not exist (it diverges). The data are perfectly separable.

examples.setup: Add an L2 penalty $0.1\,w^2$ to the same two-point problem. Is there now a best $w$?
steps: The values fall and then rise, with the minimum near $w\approx1.6$ (objective about 0.62).
examples.answer: Yes. The penalty grows with $w$ and stops the weight running away, giving a finite optimum near $w\approx1.6$.

cards.why: Maximum likelihood is why log-loss is the right loss, and the separable-data behaviour is a classic property question. In GATE: how the weights are found (iteratively, no closed form), what happens on separable data, or which loss is minimised.
how: Write the likelihood as a product over the samples.
Take $-\ln$ of it: that is the total log-loss.
Minimise it iteratively (gradient descent or Newton's method). It is convex, so the answer is global.
On perfectly separable data expect infinite weights, unless an L2 penalty is added.
cards.mistake: Believing logistic regression has a closed-form solution like $w=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$, or that separable data give finite maximum-likelihood weights. There is no closed form, and separable data push the weights to infinity.
edge_cases: Intercept only: $p=\bar y$ and $b=\ln\frac{\bar y}{1-\bar y}$.
Duplicate feature columns: the weights are not unique, but the predictions are.
Data that are not separable have a finite optimum.
L2 regularisation makes the objective strictly convex with a finite minimiser.
connections: Log-loss (an earlier card) is the quantity being minimised.
Ridge regression: the same L2 penalty fixes the separable case.
Maxima, minima and convexity: why a convex loss has one global minimum.

check.a: Yes. Gradient descent reaches the global minimum.

check.q: With separable data and no regularisation, are the best weights finite?
check.a: No. The loss keeps falling as the weights grow.

cards.title: Confusion-matrix metrics
cards.simple: After a classifier makes its guesses, sort them into four boxes. It said yes and was right (TP). It said yes and was wrong (FP). It said no but should have said yes (FN). It said no and was right (TN). From the boxes you can ask three questions. Of everything it called yes, how much was right? That is precision. Of all the real yeses, how many did it catch? That is recall. Overall, how often was it right? That is accuracy. Think of a metal detector at an airport: precision is how often a beep means real metal, and recall is how much of the real metal it catches. In exam words: precision $=TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $=TP/(TP+FN)$, accuracy $=(TP+TN)/n$.
cards.idea: A confusion matrix counts a classifier's hits and misses in a 2 by 2 table: true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN) and true negatives (TN). The usual scores come from it. **Precision** asks "of everything I called positive, how much was right?". **Recall** asks "of the real positives, how many did I find?". **Accuracy** asks "how often am I right overall?". This is outside the listed syllabus, but GATE DA 2026 asked it.
cards.definition:
$$\text{precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\quad \text{recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\quad \text{accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+FP+FN+TN},\quad F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R}$$

Symbols: TP, FP, FN, TN are the four counts. Precision divides by a column of the table (everything predicted positive). Recall divides by a row (everything actually positive). $F_1$ is the harmonic mean of precision $P$ and recall $R$.

For a two-class problem you can compute precision and recall for either class by swapping which one counts as "positive".
cards.intuition_full: Precision and recall differ only in the denominator, and each answers a different worry. High precision means few false alarms. High recall means few misses. Which matters more depends on the cost. For a disease test, missing a sick person (low recall) is worse. For a spam filter, deleting a real email (low precision) is worse. You can raise one by lowering the other: a classifier that says "positive" for everything has recall 1 but poor precision. Accuracy hides this when the classes are unbalanced. If 95 percent of cases are negative, always saying "negative" scores 95 percent accuracy while finding no positives at all. $F_1$ punishes a big gap between precision and recall, since it stays close to the smaller of the two.

example.setup: A classifier on 30 samples has TP $=12$, FN $=3$, FP $=4$, TN $=11$. Find precision, recall, accuracy and $F_1$.
steps: Lay out the table. Actual positives: $12+3=15$. Actual negatives: $4+11=15$. Predicted positive: $12+4=16$.

examples.answer: Accuracy is a flattering $0.95$ while recall is $0$. On unbalanced data, accuracy alone can hide a useless classifier.

scenes.title: The sigmoid turns a score into a probability

steps.caption: z = 0: e⁰ = 1, so p = 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5. A score of zero means a coin flip.
z = 1: e⁻¹ = 0.368, so p = 1/(1 + 0.368) = 0.731. A positive score leans toward class 1.
z = 2: e⁻² = 0.135, so p = 1/1.135 = 0.881. A bigger score gives a bigger probability, but slower.
z = −1: e¹ = 2.718, so p = 1/3.718 = 0.269. This is 1 − 0.731: the curve is symmetric about 0.5.
z = −2: e² = 7.389, so p = 1/8.389 = 0.119, which is 1 − 0.881. Never below 0, never above 1.

scenes.title: The decision boundary is a straight line

steps.caption: Take w = (1, 2) and b = −4. The score is z = x1 + 2·x2 − 4. The boundary is where z = 0, which is the straight line x1 + 2·x2 = 4.
Point A = (1, 1): z = 1 + 2 − 4 = −1, so p = σ(−1) = 0.27. Below 0.5, so class 0. It sits on the low side of the line.
Point B = (3, 2): z = 3 + 4 − 4 = 3, so p = σ(3) = 0.95. Class 1, on the high side.
Point C = (2, 1) is on the line: z = 2 + 2 − 4 = 0, so p = 0.5 exactly.
Change b to −2. The boundary x1 + 2·x2 = 2 is the same tilt, slid parallel. w sets the tilt, b slides the line. It is still a straight line.

set.text:
b = −2: same tilt,
line slides in

scenes.title: Odds, log-odds and the straight line

steps.caption: A probability of 0.6 means 0.6 for yes and 0.4 for no. The odds compare the two: 0.6 / 0.4 = 1.5, or "3 to 2".
Going back: p = odds / (1 + odds) = 1.5 / 2.5 = 0.6.
Log-odds is the natural log of the odds: ln 1.5 = 0.405. Logistic regression makes the log-odds a straight line in x. Here z = −1 + 0.5x.
At x = 2: z = −1 + 1 = 0. The odds are e⁰ = 1, so p = 0.5.
At x = 3: z = 0.5. The odds are e^0.5 = 1.65, so p = 1.65 / 2.65 = 0.62. One more unit of x added 0.5 to the log-odds and multiplied the odds by e^0.5 = 1.65.
The true label is 1 and the model says p = 0.6. The loss is −ln p = −ln 0.6 = 0.511. The curve shows the loss against the score z = ln(p/(1−p)) = 0.405.
Same p = 0.6 but the true label is 0. Now the loss is −ln(1 − p) = −ln 0.4 = 0.916. The curve flips, and the same prediction costs more.
True label 1 and p = 0.95: confident and right. The loss is −ln 0.95 = 0.051, almost nothing.
True label 1 and p = 0.05: confident and wrong. The loss is −ln 0.05 = 2.996, about 60 times bigger.
Total over the four samples: 0.511 + 0.916 + 0.051 + 2.996 = 4.474. The mean is 4.474 / 4 = 1.12. The one confident mistake supplies two thirds of it.

scenes.title: One gradient step moves the score the right way

steps.caption: One sample x = 3 with label y = 0. Weights w = 0.5, b = −1. The score is z = 0.5·3 − 1 = 0.5 and p = σ(0.5) = 0.622. The loss −ln(1 − p) = 0.974 (the dot).
The error is p − y = 0.622 − 0 = 0.622. The model is too keen on class 1, so the error is positive.
Gradients: for w it is error × x = 0.622·3 = 1.867, and for b it is the error itself, 0.622.
New score z = 0.313·3 − 1.062 = −0.122, so p = 0.469 and the loss falls from 0.974 to 0.634. The dot slid down the curve to the left.

scenes.title: XOR: no straight line separates the classes

steps.caption: Class 0 (hollow): A = (1, 1) and B = (3, 3). Class 1 (filled): C = (1, 3) and D = (3, 1). Can one straight line split them?
Try the vertical line x1 = 2 and the horizontal line x2 = 2. Each has one point of each class on both sides, so both fail.
Try the diagonal x1 + x2 = 2.5. It cuts A off alone, but B, C and D sit together on the other side, so it fails too.
Why nothing works: segment AB (class 0) and segment CD (class 1) cross at (2, 2). A line that keeps A and B on one side keeps (2, 2) there too, so C and D cannot be wholly on the other.
Fix: add the feature x1·x2. The score z = 2x1 + 2x2 − x1x2 − 4 gives A: −1, B: −1, C: +1, D: +1. A linear model in the three features separates the classes.

scenes.title: Maximum likelihood picks the smallest log-loss

steps.caption: Five labels: 1, 0, 0, 1, 1. Use a model with one probability p for every sample (intercept only, b = ln(p/(1−p))). Which p explains the labels best?

set.text: one p for all five samples

steps.caption: The likelihood multiplies the probability of each label: p·(1−p)·(1−p)·p·p = p³(1−p)². Take logs: 3 ln p + 2 ln(1−p).
Flip the sign to get the log-loss total. p = 0.2: 5.27. p = 0.4: 3.77. p = 0.6: 3.37. p = 0.8: 3.89. Smaller is better.
The smallest total is at p = 0.6, which is 3 ones out of 5. Maximising the likelihood is the same as minimising the log-loss.
In weight terms the intercept is b = ln(0.6/0.4) = ln 1.5 = 0.405.

scenes.title: Reading precision, recall and accuracy off a 2 by 2 table

steps.caption: A classifier on 30 samples. Rows are the truth, columns are what it predicted. 12 true positives (TP), 3 false negatives (FN), 4 false positives (FP), 11 true negatives (TN).
Precision looks down the "predicted +" column: of everything called positive, how many were right? 12 / (12 + 4) = 0.75.
